title: Ray and Charles Eames: More than Chairs
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro co-host voice) profile Ray and Charles Eames, the married design duo known for molded plywood and fiberglass furniture, the Eames Lounge Chair, and films like Powers of Ten. The episode covers Ray's early painting career, Charles's architecture training and Cranbrook years, their move to California, wartime work on wooden leg splints, their Venice office at 901, the Herman Miller partnership, toys and games, Case Study House No. 8, their films and exhibits, and the personal hardships and credit issues of their team. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about how new listeners should approach the back catalog.
topics: wooden leg splint World War II

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on Charles and Ray Eames and tease their design influence and furniture legacy.

segments.title: Early lives and Cranbrook
segments.summary: Ray Eames (born Bernice Alexandra Kaiser in Sacramento, 1912) is covered as a painter who studied under Hans Hofmann and was active in American Abstract Artists. Charles Eames, born in St. Louis in 1907, was an architecture student at Washington University who left, then practiced with Robert Walsh. He married Catherine Warman in 1929 and became director of the industrial design program at Cranbrook under Eliel Saarinen, where plywood experiments began.

segments.title: Plywood experiments and move to California
segments.summary: The Eames plywood chair entered the 1941 Museum of Modern Art organic design competition and won, though it was not mass producible as is. Charles and Ray married in 1941 and drove to California, where they joined the southern California modernist scene through John Entenza and Arts and Architecture magazine, designing about 26 covers.

segments.title: Kazam machine and MGM years
segments.summary: Working in broke conditions in their apartment, the couple used the Kazam machine, named after the magician-style 'kazam', to mold plywood. Charles took a job designing sets at MGM, where he met Billy Wilder, whose napping habit inspired the Eames chaise.

segments.title: Wartime leg splints and the 901 office
segments.summary: During World War II, a Navy doctor friend, Wendell Scott, asked for better wooden splints. The Eames team, with Margaret Harris and John Entenza, produced the Transportation Splint for the US Navy, with an order of about 5,000. They formed a company that was sold to Evans Products. In 1943 they opened their Venice office at 901 West Washington Boulevard, known as 901.

segments.title: Herman Miller partnership and early chairs
segments.summary: Evans Products stepped away from chair production, and the Eames team worked with Herman Miller, including George Nelson's involvement, producing the Eames Chair and later fiberglass and aluminum seating used in schools, airports and bus stations. Ray's line that what works is better than what looks good is quoted, and Ray's role in the company is discussed, including her limited public visibility.

segments.title: Eames Lounge Chair and design legacy
segments.summary: The Eames Lounge Chair, molded plywood with leather upholstery, made the couple famous and was shown on NBC's Home. Discussion covers its status as a mid-century icon, its appearance in Mad Men, the Aluminum Group chair, and the prevalence of knockoffs. Stackable designs and Antiques Roadshow appearances are also mentioned.

segments.title: Case Study House No. 8 and Ray's interior design
segments.summary: Case Study House No. 8, originally the Bridge House, was designed by Ray and Charles in the Pacific Palisades, with the meadow turned into a front yard. Ray decorated it with art objects, folk art and textiles, challenging minimalism. Case Study House No. 9 was designed with Eero Saarinen, and Neutra designed Billy Wilder's house. Ray also designed textiles such as Sea Things and the Eames Dots pattern.

segments.title: Toys, House of Cards and multimedia films
segments.summary: Eames toys included a vinyl panel construction toy from 1951 and the House of Cards deck from 1952, plus a vertical xylophone musical tower in their office. They made around 125 films and exhibits, including Powers of Ten (1977), narrated by Philip Morrison, which was based on the book Cosmic View by Kees Boeke and inspired later films.

segments.title: Personal life, credit and Charles's death
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the uncredited young designers on the Eames team, Charles's affair with Judith Wexler, and Ray's private handling of it. Charles died of a heart attack in 1978 on a consulting trip in St. Louis; Ray died of cancer on August 21, 1988, after spending a decade archiving their work.

segments.title: Short stuff and episode length
segments.summary: Hosts note that the case study house topic could be extended into a full episode, then transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: how to start with the back catalog
segments.summary: Listener Aaron Burke asks where new listeners should start. The hosts recommend the sandwich method: listen to the latest episode and the earliest, then work toward the middle.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and direct listeners to send mail to the show's address; the show credits iHeartRadio.
